persona.name: Manoj Verma
persona.background: He runs a small retail shop and has been under significant work stress recently, often skipping meals during busy days. His family notices he has become slower in thinking and less engaged over the last few months.

diagnoses.name: Overt hypothyroidism
diagnoses.description: Primary hypothyroidism with high serum TSH and low serum free T4; clinical features include lethargy, somnolence, weight gain, cold intolerance, hoarse voice, cognitive dysfunction, constipation, bradycardia, delayed tendon reflexes, and nonpitting edema (myxedema).

diagnoses.name: Myxedema madness
diagnoses.description: Severe hypothyroidism presenting with hypothermia and neuropsychiatric manifestations; can include depression and rarely dementia/psychosis with delusions and hallucinations; associated labs include hyponatremia, hypoglycemia, increased CO2, decreased WBC/Hct, increased CPK, reduced ECG voltage, respiratory acidosis with hypoxia/hypercapnia, slow-wave EEG, and elevated CSF protein (<100 mg/dL).

diagnoses.name: Subclinical hypothyroidism
diagnoses.description: Increased serum TSH with normal serum free T4; prevalent in women and elderly; can be associated with cardiovascular risk (especially when TSH >10 mU/L) and neuropsychiatric manifestations.

diagnoses.name: Sick euthyroid syndrome (Nonthyroid illness state)
diagnoses.description: Thyroid function changes in systemic illness/surgery/fasting not caused by primary thyroid or pituitary disease; most common abnormality is decreased serum total T3; TSH usually normal; treatment with thyroxine is not recommended.

diagnoses.name: Addison’s disease (Primary adrenal insufficiency)
diagnoses.description: Chronic adrenocortical insufficiency with prominent fatigue and weight loss; features include postural hypotension and salt craving, fasting hypoglycemia, hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, metabolic acidosis, and pigmentation of exposed/pressure areas and mucous membranes due to ACTH excess.

diagnoses.name: Acute adrenal crisis (Addisonian crisis)
diagnoses.description: Acute primary adrenal failure presenting with hypotension/shock out of proportion to illness severity, dehydration, acute abdomen, unexplained hypoglycemia and fever; biochemical abnormalities include hyponatremia and hyperkalemia.

diagnoses.name: Cushing’s syndrome
diagnoses.description: Clinical features include weight gain/central obesity, hypertension, purplish striae, bruising, proximal muscle weakness, emotional lability/depression/euphoria/psychosis, and glucose intolerance/diabetes; diagnosis confirmed by demonstrating inappropriate cortisol secretion not suppressed by dexamethasone.

diagnoses.name: Primary hyperparathyroidism
diagnoses.description: Often asymptomatic hypercalcemia; classic symptoms include 'moans, bones, stones, abdominal groans'—psychiatric manifestations (lethargy, fatigue, depression, confusion), bone pain/osteopenia/osteoporosis/fractures, renal stones/polyuria/polydipsia, and constipation/nausea/peptic ulcers/pancreatitis.

diagnoses.name: Thyrotoxicosis (Hyperthyroidism)
diagnoses.description: State of circulating thyroid hormone excess; classic symptoms include heat intolerance, tremor, palpitations, anxiety, weight loss, increased appetite, increased frequency of bowel movements, and shortness of breath; elderly may present with apathy, fatigue, weight loss and dominant cardiovascular/myopathic features.

diagnoses.name: Hypopituitarism (ACTH deficiency / central adrenal insufficiency)
diagnoses.description: ACTH deficiency causes weakness, nausea, vomiting, anorexia, weight loss, fever, tachycardia, and postural hypotension; severe forms can cause vascular collapse; plasma electrolytes are typically normal due to relative preservation of mineralocorticoid production and depigmentation may occur.

initialComplaint: “Doctor, I feel exhausted all the time and have lost weight recently. I also feel dizzy when I stand up.”
medicalHistory: No documented endocrine diagnosis. Over the last few months he reports vague ill health with intermittent gastrointestinal symptoms and slow recovery from minor illnesses.
symptoms:
Fatigue and weight loss are prominent. He reports dizziness suggestive of postural hypotension and a craving for salt. He also reports gastrointestinal symptoms (nausea and vomiting) and reduced appetite/anorexia. He has had episodes suggestive of fasting hypoglycemia. Family members noticed darkening of skin in exposed/pressure areas and around the mouth (pigmentation).

precomputedExplanations.description: **Overt hypothyroidism** is a state of clinically significant thyroid hormone deficiency, usually due to autoimmune thyroiditis, causing slowed metabolic processes. keySymptoms: **Fatigue** - Common in hypothyroidism due to reduced metabolic rate and decreased tissue oxygen utilization.
**Weight gain** - Typically occurs from reduced basal metabolic rate and fluid retention, not true fat loss.
**Cold intolerance** - Patients feel unusually cold because thermogenesis is reduced with low thyroid hormone.
**Constipation** - Slowed gastrointestinal motility leads to infrequent stools and abdominal bloating.
**Dry skin/coarse hair** - Reduced skin turnover and sebaceous activity cause dryness and hair changes.
**Bradycardia** - Decreased adrenergic tone and cardiac output often produce a slow heart rate.
**Myxedema** - Glycosaminoglycan deposition can cause nonpitting edema, facial puffiness, and hoarseness.

**Weight change** - Weight loss can occur from catabolism/poor intake, not from primary thyroid dysfunction.
**Abnormal TFT pattern** - Low **T3** with normal/low **T4** and non-elevated **TSH** is typical.

precomputedExplanations.description: Addison’s disease is **primary adrenal insufficiency** due to destruction or dysfunction of the adrenal cortex, causing deficiency of **cortisol**, **aldosterone**, and adrenal **androgens**. Loss of cortisol and aldosterone leads to constitutional symptoms, **postural hypotension**, electrolyte disturbances, and **hypoglycemia**, while elevated **ACTH** causes characteristic **hyperpigmentation**.
keySymptoms: **Fatigue** - Cortisol deficiency reduces energy, causing persistent tiredness and poor stress tolerance.
**Weight loss** - Chronic cortisol deficiency and anorexia lead to unintentional weight loss and cachexia.
**Postural dizziness (orthostatic symptoms)** - Aldosterone deficiency causes salt wasting and volume depletion, producing postural hypotension.
**Salt craving** - Renal sodium loss from aldosterone deficiency drives compensatory craving for salty foods.
**Nausea and vomiting** - Cortisol deficiency and electrolyte imbalance commonly cause gastrointestinal upset and vomiting.
**Reduced appetite/anorexia** - Glucocorticoid deficiency decreases appetite, contributing to weight loss and weakness.
**Fasting hypoglycemia episodes** - Low cortisol impairs gluconeogenesis, increasing risk of hypoglycemia during fasting.
**Hyperpigmentation** - High **ACTH** (and MSH activity) darkens skin in pressure areas and mucous membranes.
precomputedExplanations.clinicalReasoning: The combination of prominent **fatigue** and **weight loss** with **orthostatic dizziness**, **salt craving**, and gastrointestinal symptoms strongly suggests deficiency of both **glucocorticoids** and **mineralocorticoids**, pointing to **primary** rather than secondary adrenal insufficiency. The presence of **hyperpigmentation** in exposed/pressure areas and around the mouth supports elevated **ACTH**, a hallmark of primary adrenal failure. Expected labs (hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, metabolic acidosis, and possible hypoglycemia) match aldosterone and cortisol deficiency. Diagnostic confirmation is a low early-morning **cortisol** with elevated **ACTH** and failure of cortisol to rise on **ACTH (cosyntropin) stimulation testing**.

**Hyperkalemia** - High potassium due to aldosterone deficiency; may cause weakness and cardiac arrhythmias.
**Dehydration** - Volume depletion from salt wasting and vomiting, leading to tachycardia and orthostatic symptoms.

precomputedExplanations.description: Cushing’s syndrome is caused by chronic excess **glucocorticoids** (endogenous cortisol overproduction or exogenous steroid exposure). It typically produces a catabolic state with characteristic fat redistribution, metabolic complications, and hypertension rather than salt-wasting hypotension.

**Moon facies** - Rounded plethoric face from fat redistribution and fluid retention in hypercortisolism.
**Dorsocervical fat pad** - ‘Buffalo hump’ caused by abnormal fat deposition over upper back/neck.
**Proximal muscle weakness** - Cortisol-induced protein catabolism leads to difficulty climbing stairs or rising.
**Purple striae** - Wide violaceous abdominal striae from dermal thinning and collagen breakdown.
**Easy bruising** - Skin and vessel fragility from impaired collagen synthesis and tissue atrophy.
**Hypertension** - Cortisol increases vascular sensitivity to catecholamines and can activate mineralocorticoid receptors.
**Hyperglycemia** - Increased gluconeogenesis and insulin resistance cause diabetes or impaired glucose tolerance.
**Osteoporosis** - Bone resorption and reduced formation lead to fractures and chronic bone pain.
**Mood changes** - Depression, irritability, or cognitive changes can occur with sustained cortisol excess.
**Infections** - Immunosuppression predisposes to recurrent or severe infections and poor wound healing.

missingFindings: **Hypercalcemia** - Expected hallmark; absence makes PTH-driven disease unlikely in this presentation.
**Renal stones (nephrolithiasis)** - Common clinical clue; not suggested by history or exam here.
**Bone disease** - Bone pain, fractures, or low bone density would support PTH excess; not described.
**Hypophosphatemia** - Typical biochemical pattern in primary hyperparathyroidism; not expected in this case.

precomputedExplanations.description: **Thyrotoxicosis** is a clinical state caused by excess circulating thyroid hormones (T3/T4), producing a hypermetabolic, hyperadrenergic syndrome. Common causes include **Graves disease**, toxic multinodular goiter, and thyroiditis, leading to systemic symptoms affecting cardiovascular, neuromuscular, and gastrointestinal systems.
keySymptoms: **Heat intolerance** - Feeling excessively warm with preference for cool environments due to increased thermogenesis.
**Weight loss with increased appetite** - Catabolic state causes weight loss despite eating more than usual.
**Palpitations** - Awareness of rapid or forceful heartbeat from **tachycardia** and increased beta-adrenergic tone.
**Tremor** - Fine postural tremor from heightened sympathetic activity and increased neuromuscular excitability.
**Anxiety/irritability** - Restlessness, insomnia, and emotional lability due to CNS stimulation.
**Increased sweating** - Excess perspiration from elevated basal metabolic rate and sympathetic activation.
**Frequent stools/diarrhea** - Increased gut motility causing loose stools rather than persistent vomiting.
**Proximal muscle weakness** - Difficulty climbing stairs or rising from a chair due to thyrotoxic myopathy.
**Menstrual irregularity** - Oligomenorrhea or amenorrhea from altered gonadotropin dynamics (in females).
**Goiter** - Enlarged thyroid, often with bruit in **Graves disease** due to increased vascularity.
precomputedExplanations.clinicalReasoning: Thyrotoxicosis typically presents with a hypermetabolic picture: **heat intolerance**, **tachycardia**, **tremor**, **sweating**, and often **increased appetite** with weight loss. Orthostatic symptoms can occur from volume depletion, but classic thyrotoxicosis does not produce **hyperpigmentation** or prominent **salt craving**. Biochemically, thyrotoxicosis is characterized by **suppressed TSH** with elevated **free T4/T3**, not low morning cortisol with elevated ACTH. The patient’s constellation (postural hypotension, pigmentation, salt craving, hypoglycemia) aligns far more strongly with **primary adrenal insufficiency** than thyroid hormone excess.
precomputedExplanations.whyIncorrectForCase: This patient has **hyperpigmentation**, **salt craving**, **postural hypotension**, and episodes of **fasting hypoglycemia**, which are classic for **Addison’s disease** and not typical of thyrotoxicosis. Expected Addison-type labs (**hyponatremia**, **hyperkalemia**, low AM cortisol with high ACTH, failed cosyntropin response) directly contradict the diagnostic framework of hyperthyroidism.
keyDifferencesFromCorrect: **Skin changes** - Thyrotoxicosis causes warm, moist skin; Addison’s causes **diffuse hyperpigmentation** (ACTH excess).
**Blood pressure physiology** - Thyrotoxicosis often has widened pulse pressure; Addison’s causes **hypotension/orthostasis** from mineralocorticoid deficiency.
**Electrolytes** - Thyrotoxicosis usually has no characteristic hyperkalemia; Addison’s has **hyponatremia**, **hyperkalemia**, and **metabolic acidosis**.
**Glucose tendency** - Thyrotoxicosis may worsen glucose tolerance; Addison’s predisposes to **fasting hypoglycemia**.
**Hormonal pattern** - Thyrotoxicosis: **low TSH, high T4/T3**; Addison’s: **low cortisol, high ACTH**, poor response to **cosyntropin**.
**Cravings** - Salt craving is not a feature of thyrotoxicosis; it is typical in Addison’s due to aldosterone deficiency.
missingFindings: **Tachycardia/atrial fibrillation** - Common in thyrotoxicosis; absence makes thyroid excess less likely here.
**Heat intolerance and sweating** - Expected hyperadrenergic symptoms; not reported in this presentation.
**Fine tremor** - Typical neuromuscular sign of thyrotoxicosis; not described in the case.
**Goiter or thyroid eye signs** - **Goiter**, **lid lag**, or **ophthalmopathy** would support Graves-related thyrotoxicosis.
**Suppressed TSH with elevated free T4/T3** - Key diagnostic labs for thyrotoxicosis; case instead suggests low cortisol and high ACTH.

precomputedExplanations.description: **Central adrenal insufficiency** results from inadequate pituitary **ACTH** secretion, leading to low adrenal **cortisol** production. Because **aldosterone** is largely regulated by the renin–angiotensin system, mineralocorticoid deficiency is usually absent, and **ACTH-driven hyperpigmentation** does not occur.
keySymptoms: **Fatigue** - Chronic low **cortisol** reduces energy, causing persistent tiredness and reduced exercise tolerance.
**Weight loss** - Appetite reduction and catabolic effects from hormonal deficiency can lead to gradual weight loss.
**Postural dizziness** - Low **cortisol** can impair vascular tone, contributing to orthostatic symptoms without severe hyperkalemia.
**Nausea/vomiting** - **Cortisol** deficiency can cause nonspecific gastrointestinal upset and poor oral intake.
**Fasting hypoglycemia** - Reduced gluconeogenesis from low **cortisol** predisposes to hypoglycemia, especially during fasting/illness.
**Low morning cortisol** - Early morning **cortisol** is low due to insufficient pituitary stimulation of the adrenal cortex.
precomputedExplanations.clinicalReasoning: This diagnosis could explain fatigue, weight loss, nausea, and episodes of fasting hypoglycemia via **cortisol deficiency**. Orthostatic symptoms may occur because **cortisol** supports catecholamine-mediated vascular responsiveness. However, central adrenal insufficiency typically has **low/normal ACTH**, lacks **hyperpigmentation**, and usually does not produce prominent **mineralocorticoid deficiency** findings. Therefore, the overall pattern in this patient is more consistent with primary adrenal failure rather than pituitary ACTH deficiency.
precomputedExplanations.whyIncorrectForCase: The patient has clear **hyperpigmentation** (exposed/pressure areas and mucosa), which implies **elevated ACTH** and argues against ACTH deficiency. He also has features suggesting **mineralocorticoid deficiency** (salt craving, expected **hyponatremia**, **hyperkalemia**, **metabolic acidosis**), which are typical of Addison’s disease but not central adrenal insufficiency.
keyDifferencesFromCorrect: **ACTH level** - Central adrenal insufficiency has **low/normal ACTH**; Addison’s has **high ACTH** from loss of negative feedback.
**Pigmentation** - Central disease lacks **hyperpigmentation**; Addison’s causes pigmentation via excess **ACTH/MSH** activity.
**Aldosterone status** - Central disease usually preserves **aldosterone**; Addison’s causes **aldosterone deficiency** with salt wasting.
**Electrolytes** - Central disease typically lacks **hyperkalemia** and severe **metabolic acidosis**; Addison’s commonly has both.
**Salt craving** - Uncommon in central adrenal insufficiency; common in Addison’s due to **sodium loss** and volume depletion.
**Cosyntropin response** - Central disease may show a delayed/partial response if adrenals are not atrophic; Addison’s shows **failure of cortisol rise** due to adrenal destruction.
missingFindings: **Low/normal ACTH** - Absence of low ACTH (and presence of pigmentation suggesting high ACTH) argues against central insufficiency.
**No hyperkalemia** - Central adrenal insufficiency should not cause marked **hyperkalemia** because **aldosterone** is preserved.

**No mineralocorticoid deficiency signs** - Lack of expected salt-wasting pattern (salt craving, volume depletion with hyperkalemia/acidosis) would support central disease, but this case suggests the opposite.
**Other pituitary hormone deficits** - Hypopituitarism often coexists with **hypothyroidism**, **hypogonadism**, or pituitary mass symptoms; these are not described here.

keyHistoryQuestions.action: Ask about fatigue/exhaustion and recent weight loss
keyHistoryQuestions.reasoning: These are described as the most prominent symptoms in Addison’s disease and directly match the patient’s presenting complaint.
keyHistoryQuestions.expectedFinding: Persistent fatigue with unintentional weight loss
keyHistoryQuestions.textbookReference: “Fatigue and weight loss are the most prominent symptoms.”

keyHistoryQuestions.action: Ask about dizziness on standing / postural symptoms suggestive of hypotension
keyHistoryQuestions.reasoning: Chronic primary adrenal failure may present with features suggestive of postural hypotension; hypotension is also a cardinal feature.
keyHistoryQuestions.expectedFinding: Dizziness on standing consistent with postural hypotension
keyHistoryQuestions.textbookReference: “features suggestive of postural hypotension” and “Cardinal features of Addison’s disease: Hypotension…”

keyHistoryQuestions.reasoning: Salt craving is listed under mineralocorticoid deficiency and is a typical chronic presentation clue.
keyHistoryQuestions.expectedFinding: Craving for salty foods / desire to add extra salt
keyHistoryQuestions.textbookReference: “salt craving” and “Chronic: … features suggestive of postural hypotension and salt craving.”

keyHistoryQuestions.action: Ask about gastrointestinal symptoms (anorexia, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea or constipation)
keyHistoryQuestions.reasoning: GI symptoms are listed among chronic features and glucocorticoid deficiency manifestations.
keyHistoryQuestions.expectedFinding: Anorexia with nausea/vomiting and/or bowel habit change
keyHistoryQuestions.textbookReference: “vague features of ill health, sometimes including gastrointestinal symptoms” and “anorexia, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea or constipation”

keyHistoryQuestions.action: Ask about any previous episode of acute adrenal crisis after stress (infection, trauma, surgery, dehydration due to vomiting/diarrhea or salt deprivation) or slow recovery from illness
keyHistoryQuestions.reasoning: A prior stress-related crisis or slow recovery is listed as a cardinal feature and supports the diagnosis of Addison’s disease.
keyHistoryQuestions.expectedFinding: History of hypotension/shock out of proportion to illness or slow recovery after illness/stress
keyHistoryQuestions.textbookReference: “Cardinal features of Addison’s disease: … previous history of acute adrenal crisis following stress, or slow recovery from illness.”

keyExaminations.action: Measure blood pressure and assess for hypotension (including postural component)
keyExaminations.reasoning: Hypotension is a cardinal feature and is also listed under mineralocorticoid deficiency; postural symptoms are part of chronic presentation.
keyExaminations.expectedFinding: Hypotension and/or postural drop in blood pressure
keyExaminations.textbookReference: “Cardinal features of Addison’s disease: Hypotension…” and “Hypotension… Dizziness”

keyExaminations.action: Inspect for hyperpigmentation of exposed and pressure areas (elbows, knees, knuckles), palmar creases, and recently acquired scars
keyExaminations.reasoning: Skin pigmentation is nearly always present in primary adrenal insufficiency (not in secondary) and is due to ACTH excess.
keyExaminations.expectedFinding: Diffuse/patchy hyperpigmentation in typical sites (including palmar creases and scars)
keyExaminations.textbookReference: “Skin pigmentation is nearly always present in primary adrenal insufficiency (but not in secondary).” and “Pigmentation of exposed areas, pressure areas… palmar creases… recently acquired scars”

keyExaminations.reasoning: Oral pigmentation is specifically illustrated as a feature of Addison’s disease and supports ACTH-excess pigmentation.
keyExaminations.textbookReference: “FIGS. 13.17A AND B: … Oral pigmentation in Addison’s disease.”

keyExaminations.action: Assess body weight/nutritional status for weight loss and anorexia
keyExaminations.reasoning: Weight loss and anorexia are listed among prominent/chronic features and support clinical suspicion prior to biochemical confirmation.
keyExaminations.expectedFinding: Low weight or documented weight loss
keyExaminations.textbookReference: “Fatigue and weight loss are the most prominent symptoms.” and “Weight loss and anorexia”

keyInvestigations.action: Order serum electrolytes and glucose (and blood urea as part of routine labs)
keyInvestigations.reasoning: Addisonian crisis and chronic adrenal insufficiency are associated with electrolyte abnormalities and hypoglycemia; the crisis protocol explicitly includes electrolytes and glucose, and the textbook lists hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, hypoglycemia, and elevated blood urea.
keyInvestigations.expectedFinding: Hyponatremia and hyperkalemia; hypoglycemia; elevated blood urea (azotemia)
keyInvestigations.textbookReference: “Laboratory Findings: Hyponatremia, Hyperkalemia… Hypoglycemia… Azotemia” and “Hypoglycemia, elevated blood urea, hyponatremia, and hyperkalemia.”

keyInvestigations.action: Measure early morning (6 am) serum cortisol
keyInvestigations.reasoning: This is the first-line biochemical test described, with clear cutoffs for suggesting or excluding adrenal insufficiency.
keyInvestigations.expectedFinding: Cortisol <3 µg/dL suggestive of adrenal insufficiency; cortisol >11 µg/dL excludes adrenal insufficiency
keyInvestigations.textbookReference: “Early morning (6 am) cortisol level… Levels <3 µg/dL is suggestive of adrenal insufficiency… Levels >11 µg/dL exclude AI.”

keyInvestigations.reasoning: ACTH is elevated in adrenal insufficiency and helps determine whether cortisol deficiency is primary (adrenal) versus central.
keyInvestigations.expectedFinding: Elevated plasma ACTH in adrenal insufficiency
keyInvestigations.textbookReference: “Plasma ACTH level: Elevated in adrenal insufficiency.” and “Determine whether the cortisol deficiency is primary or central AI.”

keyInvestigations.action: Perform ACTH stimulation test using 0.25 mg (standard high dose) synthetic ACTH (cosyntropin) with cortisol measurement
keyInvestigations.reasoning: The textbook states that failure of cortisol to rise after cosyntropin confirms adrenal insufficiency.
keyInvestigations.expectedFinding: Failure of rise in plasma cortisol following administration of 0.25 mg synthetic ACTH
keyInvestigations.textbookReference: “ACTH stimulation test: There is failure of rise in plasma cortisol level following the administration of 0.25 mg… of synthetic ACTH (cosyntropin).”

keyInvestigations.action: If evaluating etiology (especially suspected tuberculous adrenalitis), order imaging/radiology: chest radiograph and adrenal imaging (plain abdominal radiograph, CT scan, MRI) to look for adrenal calcification
keyInvestigations.reasoning: Radiographic evaluation is described for tuberculous adrenalitis, including chest evidence of pulmonary TB and adrenal calcification on abdominal radiograph/CT/MRI.
keyInvestigations.expectedFinding: Chest radiograph evidence of pulmonary tuberculosis; adrenal gland calcification on plain radiograph/CT/MRI
keyInvestigations.textbookReference: “Radiograph: In patients with tuberculous adrenalitis: Chest radiograph may show evidences of pulmonary tuberculosis and plain radiograph of abdomen, CT scan, and MRI scan may show calcification in the adrenal gland.”

differentialDiagnoses.name: Secondary (central) adrenal insufficiency
differentialDiagnoses.howToRuleOut: Look for absence of pigmentation (pigmentation is nearly always present in primary but not in secondary) and use plasma ACTH to determine whether cortisol deficiency is primary or central.
differentialDiagnoses.textbookReference: “Skin pigmentation is nearly always present in primary adrenal insufficiency (but not in secondary).” and “Determine whether the cortisol deficiency is primary or central AI.”

differentialDiagnoses.name: Acute adrenal crisis (Addisonian crisis) vs chronic presentation
differentialDiagnoses.howToRuleOut: Differentiate by acute features (shock out of proportion to illness, dehydration, ‘acute abdomen’, unexplained hypoglycemia and fever) versus chronic vague ill health with postural hypotension and salt craving.
differentialDiagnoses.textbookReference: “Acute: Hypotension and acute circulatory failure with shock… dehydration, an ‘acute abdomen’, unexplained hypoglycemia, and unexplained fever (Addisonian crisis)” and “Chronic: Vague features… postural hypotension and salt craving.”

differentialDiagnoses.name: Ectopic ACTH-related pigmentation (as a cause of pigmentation)
differentialDiagnoses.howToRuleOut: Consider ectopic ACTH secretion when pigmentation occurs with impaired glucose tolerance and hypokalemic alkalosis (rather than the hyponatremia/hyperkalemia pattern described in adrenal insufficiency).
differentialDiagnoses.textbookReference: “Ectopic ACTH Secretion… Impaired glucose tolerance… Hypokalemic alkalosis… Skin pigmentation” and (for adrenal crisis labs) “Hyponatremia… Hyperkalemia… Hypoglycemia.”

differentialDiagnoses.name: Polyglandular autoimmune syndromes associated with Addison’s disease (contextual differential/association)
differentialDiagnoses.howToRuleOut: Screen clinically for associated autoimmune diseases and recognize syndromic patterns: Type I (adrenal insufficiency + hypoparathyroidism + chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis) and Type II/Schmidt (Addison’s disease + Hashimoto’s thyroiditis).
differentialDiagnoses.textbookReference: “Other autoimmune diseases associated with Addison’s disease…” and “Type I polyglandular autoimmune syndrome…” and “Type II polyglandular autoimmune syndrome/Schmidt syndrome…”

idealPathway.diagnosticApproach: Use the textbook three-step process: (1) Suspect primary adrenal insufficiency clinically (fatigue and weight loss; chronic postural hypotension and salt craving; pigmentation) and assess for crisis features if acutely ill. (2) Confirm adrenal insufficiency by demonstrating inappropriately low cortisol secretion (early morning 6 am cortisol; if needed ACTH stimulation test showing failure of cortisol rise). (3) Determine whether cortisol deficiency is primary or central using plasma ACTH (pigmentation supports primary; ACTH elevated in adrenal insufficiency), then determine the cause (e.g., tuberculous adrenalitis with chest radiograph and adrenal imaging showing calcification; consider adrenal autoantibodies such as ACA and anti-21-OH-hydroxylase antibody).
